content.text:
I submitted **part-based** with confidence 0.85, using 39 of the 60 budget.

**Design.** I trained the learner on three tasks, L1-S1-M1, L2-S2-M2 and L3-S3-M3, so every rule it learned appeared in exactly one task. A factor-when-justified learner (whether k is 2 or 3) therefore has no reusable parts yet and should behave like the holistic one. That leaves one question: does the cost of a new task follow the number of new rules, or how similar the task is to the trained ones? I then tested tasks where those two factors point in opposite directions.

**Results** (examples to reach criterion, averaged over repeated tests):

| New rules | Tasks tested | Max similarity to a trained task | Tests | Mean examples |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | L1-S2-M3, L3-S1-M2, L2-S1-M3 | 0.375 | 14 | 20 |
| 1 | L1-S4-M1, L2-S4-M2, L3-S4-M3 | 0.625 | 10 | 30 |
| 2 | L4-S4-M1 | 0.56 | 6 | 37 |
| 3 | L4-S4-M4 | 0.19 | 5 | 46 |

Cost rose steadily with the number of new rules. The tasks recombining only trained rules were the cheapest, even though they were less similar to the trained tasks than the others. A holistic learner, or a factor-when-justified learner that has no parts yet, predicts the reverse.

**Caveats:**
- The noise is large: single tests of the same task ranged from 1 to 43.
- The one-new-rule group was mixed. L1-S4-M1 averaged 37, but L2-S4-M2 and L3-S4-M3 came in around 17–21 from only two tests each, which is close to the recombination tasks.
- The cleanest contrast is L4-S4-M1 against the recombinations, at about 2.5 standard errors.
- I never ran the follow-up (training rules into 2–3 tasks) that would test factor-when-justified directly. That's why I put confidence at 0.85 rather than higher.
